transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-21
Start time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Sara Martinez (Redwood SE), Victor Nguyen (Argon - Head of ML), Priya Shah (Argon - CTO), Luca Romano (Argon - SRE)

Summary (auto): Quick discovery to understand Argon's model selection needs across Hosted/Dedicated/Private. Main topics: context length needs (long documents), multilingual support, tool-calling/function-calling, security/VPC, and benchmarking next steps.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya Chen, AE at Redwood. With me is Sara Martinez, our solutions engineer. How's everybody doing?
[00:08] Victor: Good, thanks. Excited to, uh, dig in. We have about, I think, 45 minutes?
[00:12] Maya: We've got about 50 — the invite says 52 — so should be good. Quick agenda: understand your workloads, context length, multilingual needs, whether Hosted/Dedicated/Private fits, and next steps for a benchmark.
[00:25] Priya: Sounds good. For context, Argon builds autonomy software for inspection drones, we ingest long flight logs, multi-modal later but mostly large fused text for now — and we need long context and reliable tool-calls to hit external APIs.
[00:40] Sara: Great, that helps. Just to clarify, when you say long context, what's typical? Token-wise or doc-wise?
[00:46] Victor: Average is about 12k tokens per request, spikes up to 50k in full session replays. Usually we chunk but would prefer a model that can handle 32k or more to reduce prompt engineering.
[00:58] Luca: And we need function-calling like calling our telemetry API and a reranker for candidate actions. Latency goal is sub-600ms for interactive controls; batch jobs can be higher.
[01:10] Sara: That makes sense. So the tradeoff we're going to discuss is context length vs latency vs cost. For 32k+ you usually look at 8-bit quantization or specifically quantized variants and sometimes Dedicated pools for throughput.
[01:25] Victor: Can you run through the open models you support on Hosted and whether Dedicated allows larger contexts? I saw a doc but some names were garbled — Redwood Dedicade, Redwood privatee — sorry, transcription issues.
[01:36] Maya: (laughs) Totally fine. On Hosted we surface a model catalog — we have curated open models like Mistral variants, LlamaX forks, and some long-context tuned models. Dedicated gives you the option to pin larger-context variants and we can enable longer KV cache and memory configs. Private (VPC/on-prem) is for when you need customer-managed keys and air-gapped setup.
[01:55] Priya: How about multilingual? We have crews in EMEA and Latin America, so Spanish/Portuguese are musts, plus noise in transcripts so robustness matters.
[02:03] Sara: We typically recommend models that are trained with multilingual corpora — some open models have strong English performance but weaker Spanish. We can run your sample sets through a quick eval to show relative quality.
[02:12] Victor: And tool-calling — function calling — do all the models support structured function outputs, or is that a Redwood runtime feature?
[02:20] Sara: The runtime adds structured output tooling — wrappers and stable parsing — but support depends on the base model's ability to produce structured JSON reliably. For many open models we have a deterministic post-processing layer and guardrails to help. In Dedicated/Private you can also run function-calling proxies with lower latency.
[02:36] Priya: Any differences in SLOs between Hosted and Dedicated? We're concerned about predictable latency for live control.
[02:42] Maya: Hosted has shared capacity with per-customer priority; Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and predictable throughput. We offer SLA-backed targets for Dedicated — latency and uptime SLAs — and autoscaling policies.
[02:52] Luca: Does Dedicated let us pick instance types? Like A100 vs H100 presets? Our infra prefers H100 for throughput.
[02:58] Sara: Yes, Dedicated pools can be provisioned on specific hardware classes when you commit. For H100 we can optimize kernel selection and compilation to squeeze latency out.
[03:06] Victor: On cost — our CFO will want a sense of per-token economics. Any ballpark for 32k windows?
[03:12] Maya: Ballparks vary — hosted long-context models are higher per-token; Dedicated amortizes cost across the pool — with batching and caching we often see 30–60% reductions in per-token unit cost for steady throughput. We'll share a spreadsheet.
[03:24] Priya: We will need SOC2 and ISO documents, and KMS/HSM support — do you have enterprise packages?
[03:30] Maya: Yes, enterprise/private includes SOC2, ISO artifacts, and KMS integrations. We'll attach the security pack.
[03:35] Victor: For the benchmark, we want to compare Redwood hosted vs our in-house LlamaX fork vs Anthropic-style model. Can Redwood run a head-to-head with our sample dataset?
[03:44] Sara: Absolutely. We can run three configs: Hosted long-context, Dedicated with quantized model, and Private on your VPC (if you want). We just need the sample prompts, expected outputs, and latency/cost targets.
[03:56] Luca: Regarding VPC, we need to ensure peering and egress rules — we can't have outbound to unknown IPs. Is there a network diagram we can review?
[04:03] Maya: We'll include our VPC peering guide and typical firewall ports. For Private we support customer-managed networking and can do on-prem too.
[04:10] Priya: A couple of technical questions — 1) How do you handle KV cache eviction for long sessions? 2) Is continuous batching configurable per route so we can isolate control-plane latency from bulk inference?
[04:20] Sara: Great questions. KV cache is managed per-request with pinning policies for active sessions; we support prefix caching for repeated chunks. Continuous batching is configurable — you can set per-route latency SLOs and batching thresholds so critical routes hit lower queue times.
[04:32] Victor: Are some models better at tool-calling? We had poor JSON outputs from a prior open model.
[04:37] Sara: Yes, model architecture and decoding temperature affect structured outputs. Deterministic decoding, prompt templates, and post-hoc validation help. We can also run a reranker model to validate JSON before returning it to your control system.
[04:49] Priya: How about fine-tuning vs instruction-tuning vs retrieval augmentation for our domain? We're exploring RAG for memory-heavy tasks.
[04:57] Maya: RAG is a solid approach for long-term memory. For immediate session windows, long-context models reduce the need to retrieve, but RAG helps with efficiency and cheaper models. We support managed vector stores and embeddings pipelines on Hosted and give connectors for Dedicated/Private.
[05:10] Victor: Any constraints around PII or telemetry? We need audit logs and data residency in EU for some customers.
[05:15] Maya: We have audit trails in Redwood Console, retention controls, and regional hosting for EU. Private deployments are best when you need strict residency and control.
[05:23] Luca: For an initial POC, what's the typical stack? We want to do a small pilot: 1) Redwood hosted eval for 2 weeks, 2) then Dedicated benchmark with 2-node H100 pool. Is that doable?
[05:33] Sara: Totally doable. We usually start with Hosted eval to validate quality and tools, then move to a Dedicated/benchmark run. We'll capture token/cost/latency metrics.
[05:40] Victor: Ok, walk me through function-calling flow — we want to call an internal API that controls drone motors; safety is critical. How do you prevent hallucinated calls or malformed payloads?
[05:50] Sara: We recommend a strict schema for function payloads, server-side validators, and a middleware that validates signatures and parameter ranges. On Dedicated/Private we can additionally run validators in-line to block unsafe commands. Also, use canary testing and simulated actuators for initial rollouts.
[06:06] Priya: Are there any known limitations with 50k token spikes? I know some runtimes trade off throughput.
[06:12] Sara: At 50k you hit memory and KV constraints; we typically shard or stream responses. Some long-context variants support chunked KV cache to scale beyond native limits, but it increases end-to-end latency. For interactive sub-600ms you probably need a trimmed 32k window and carefully engineered prompts.
[06:27] Victor: On multilingual — have you benchmarked Spanish generation? We need high-quality Spanish summaries from noisy transcripts.
[06:33] Sara: We have multilingual model benches — in general, some open models do well for Spanish with finetuning; we can run your test set and show BLEU/ROUGE-like metrics and human eval notes.
[06:45] Maya: Quick interjection — a couple of items we'll include in the follow-up: security pack, VPC guide, pricing sheet, and a recommended benchmark plan with configs (models, context lengths, hardware).
[06:56] Priya: Great. For the benchmark configs, can you include 1) a high-quality larger model at 32k on Hosted, 2) a quantized Dedicated run, and 3) a RAG-augmented cheaper model?
[07:06] Sara: Yep, that's standard. We'll propose models and expected throughput.
[07:10] Victor: Any red flags on our side? We're considering both Dedicated and Private because compliance might require Private eventually.
[07:16] Maya: No red flags — it sounds like a normal enterprise path: start Hosted eval, validate quality and latency with your prompts, then Dedicated for predictable SLOs, and Private only if residency/compliance or air-gap is necessary.
[07:26] Luca: For Private, what's the deployment model? Agent installs in our VPC or you ship a package?
[07:30] Sara: We offer a Private control plane with customer-managed networking — typically a hybrid: control plane in our region but connectors and model runtime can be in your VPC or on-prem. For air-gapped we provide an on-prem bundle.
[07:40] Victor: Ok, timeline — we want to pick a vendor within 6 weeks. What's the fastest path to a meaningful POC?
[07:47] Maya: Fastest is Hosted eval with 2-week access, sample dataset, and a lightweight benchmark. We can have results in 10 business days once we get samples.
[07:55] Priya: Cost for the eval?
[07:57] Maya: We can grant eval credits for hosted — will confirm amount in follow-up. Dedicated benchmarking typically needs a paid commitment for node hours, but we'll quote a small bench rate.
[08:06] Victor: A quick question about integrations — we use SSO (Okta) and SCIM for provisioning. Do you support that for Redwood console?
[08:13] Maya: Yes, SSO/SAML and SCIM provisioning are supported for enterprise accounts. We'll include the SSO setup guide.
[08:20] Priya: Any rate-limiting controls? We want per-route quotas so model-heavy routes can't starve control routes.
[08:25] Sara: Per-route throttles and token-level limits are supported; Console gives per-route dashboards and can set lower latency buckets.
[08:32] Victor: On the security artifacts, do you have pen-test reports?
[08:36] Maya: We have a pen-test summary in our security pack and can share higher-level findings under NDA.
[08:43] Luca: Technical nit: what's your observability like? We need token-level breakdowns and end-to-end tracing into our API calls.
[08:51] Sara: Redwood Console has token-level cost/latency breakdowns, request traces, and per-model dashboards. You can hook tracing into your logging system.
[08:58] Priya: Ok, that's helpful. I want to talk about function-calling reliability — can we do a short demo next week focusing on tool-calls?
[09:05] Maya: Yes, we should set up a demo, likely SE-led, with your sample APIs. Sara, can you own that?
[09:09] Sara: Yep, I can run a demo showing function-calling, JSON validation, and reranker flows. We'll also show Dedicated config differences.
[09:16] Victor: Great. A few minutes left — let's recap next steps.
[09:20] Maya: Recap: 1) We'll send security pack, pricing sheet, and VPC guide (Maya). 2) Sara will share benchmark config and request sample dataset (Sara). 3) Argon will provide sample prompts, transcripts, and latency targets (Victor). 4) Luca will confirm VPC/network requirements. 5) Schedule function-calling demo next week (Sara + Argon).
[09:36] Priya: That matches our notes.
[09:38] Victor: Any competitors or procurement traps we should be aware of? We're also running internal cost models vs Bedrock and Anthropic.
[09:45] Maya: We're used to that — we'll provide comparative benchmarks where available but mostly focus on your sample-lab run.
[09:50] Sara: One more technical note — for the reranker and safety checks we usually recommend a small in-house model to validate outputs before actuator steps; keeps latency tight.
[09:58] Luca: Makes sense.
[10:00] Maya: Ok team, thanks for your time; we'll follow up by EOD tomorrow with the docs and schedule.
[10:06] Priya: Thanks, bye.
[10:08] Victor: Thanks, bye.
[10:10] End of recording.
